blocks.text: 1. Batch Gradient Descent
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931449-939919946.png

Gradient Descent, already shared with the traditional Machine Learning course, describes the general idea of adjusting weights to reduce loss. Batch Gradient Descent is the specific version that uses the entire training dataset for every single weight update.

It is the first of three genuinely distinct variants covered across this module, Batch, Stochastic, and Mini-Batch, each one differing based on exactly how much data actually feeds into each individual update step.
2. The Mechanism
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931449-561202824.png
Batch Gradient Descent computes the gradient using every single training example, all at once, then averages those individual gradients together into one single, combined update.

It updates every weight exactly once using that single averaged gradient, then repeats the entire process, meaning one full pass through the entire dataset corresponds to exactly one single weight update, a genuinely important detail worth keeping clear.

blocks.text: 3. A Genuine Accuracy Advantage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931449-419813642.png
A genuine advantage of using the full dataset for every update is that the computed gradient is a genuinely accurate, low-noise estimate of the true direction that actually reduces the loss.

Since every single training example contributes to each update, the resulting gradient reflects the true, overall pattern across the entire dataset, rather than being skewed by whatever small, potentially unrepresentative subset happened to be used for any single step.
4. A Genuine Speed Weakness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931450-402828040.png

This connects back to the batch concept already covered in The Deep Learning Workflow topic. One single weight update requires processing the entire dataset first, meaning for a genuinely large dataset, this results in very few weight updates per unit of actual, real time.

Training can become genuinely, impractically slow at real-world scale under this constraint, since a network might need thousands of weight updates to actually converge, and each one requires a full pass through potentially millions of training examples.
5. A Genuine Memory Constraint
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931451-431892560.png
A genuine, practical constraint is that computing the gradient over the entire dataset at once requires holding, or at least processing, the entire dataset in memory simultaneously.

This is genuinely impractical for datasets too large to fit available memory, a real, concrete limitation that alone can rule out Batch Gradient Descent entirely for many genuinely large, real-world training datasets, regardless of how much time might otherwise be available for training.

blocks.content: This memory constraint alone often rules out Batch Gradient Descent for real-world datasets, well before its speed weakness, already covered in the previous section, even becomes the deciding factor.

blocks.text: 6. A Smooth, Predictable Convergence

This connects back to a loss curve's shape, an idea implicit throughout much of this course so far. Batch Gradient Descent's loss decreases smoothly, with essentially no noise from update to update, a genuinely clean, predictable path toward the minimum.

This smoothness is a direct, natural consequence of the accuracy advantage already covered earlier in this topic, since every single update uses the exact same, complete, low-noise gradient estimate, producing a genuinely consistent, steady decrease in loss over time.
7. Where Stochastic Gradient Descent Came From

blocks.alt: Where Stochastic Gradient Descent Came From
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931451-322279376.png

This connects forward to Stochastic Gradient Descent, already shared with the traditional Machine Learning course. It was developed specifically to address Batch Gradient Descent's genuine speed and memory weaknesses, both already covered earlier in this topic.

It does this by using one single example per update, instead of the entire dataset, a dramatically different tradeoff that directly trades away Batch's accuracy advantage in exchange for considerably faster, more frequent weight updates.

blocks.text: 8. A Preview of Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

This connects forward to Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, the very next topic in this module. It offers a genuinely practical middle ground between Batch's full dataset and Stochastic's single example, covered fully in that immediately following topic.

Understanding Batch Gradient Descent's genuine strengths and weaknesses clearly now, covered fully throughout this topic, sets up direct, considerable groundwork for understanding exactly why this middle-ground approach actually became the standard, practical default in modern Deep Learning practice.
9. Recognizing When Batch Gradient Descent Still Fits

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Batch Gradient Descent Still Fits
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444931453-722861352.png

A genuinely small dataset, comfortably fitting in memory, is a genuine case where Batch Gradient Descent still fits well today, its accuracy advantage, already covered throughout this topic, genuinely worth the speed tradeoff at this smaller, more manageable scale.

Any genuinely large, real-world dataset instead generally finds Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered in the very next topic, the far more common, practical choice, balancing accuracy and speed considerably better than either extreme.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements Batch Gradient Descent from scratch, computing one averaged gradient across the entire dataset per weight update.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 1))
y = 3 * X.ravel() + 2 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200)  # true relationship: y = 3x + 2

weight, bias = 0.0, 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
epochs = 20

for epoch in range(epochs):
    predictions = weight * X.ravel() + bias
    errors = predictions - y

    # Gradients computed using the ENTIRE dataset, exactly the batch approach covered in this topic
    gradient_weight = np.mean(errors * X.ravel())
    gradient_bias = np.mean(errors)

    weight -= learning_rate * gradient_weight
    bias -= learning_rate * gradient_bias

    if epoch % 5 == 0:
        loss = np.mean(errors ** 2)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch}: weight={weight:.4f}, bias={bias:.4f}, loss={loss:.4f}")

print(f"\nFinal: weight={weight:.4f}, bias={bias:.4f} (true values: weight=3.0, bias=2.0)")
print("Each epoch used the entire 200-example dataset for exactly one weight update")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice this example computes np.mean across the entire dataset for every single gradient calculation, exactly the full-dataset averaging covered throughout this topic, resulting in just one weight update per full pass through all 200 examples.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Batch Gradient Descent uses the entire training dataset for every single weight update.
It computes the gradient over every example, averages them, and updates weights once per full pass.
Using the full dataset produces a genuinely accurate, low-noise gradient estimate.
One weight update requires processing the entire dataset, making training genuinely slow at real-world scale.
It requires the entire dataset to fit in memory at once, genuinely impractical for very large datasets.
Its loss decreases smoothly, with essentially no noise, a direct consequence of its accuracy advantage.
Stochastic Gradient Descent was developed specifically to address these speed and memory weaknesses.
Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered next, offers a practical middle ground between the two extremes.
Next up: Stochastic Gradient Descent, already shared with the traditional ML course, using one example per update.
